5.frame: Audit item [ID] concerns [exact sentence or citation]. [Matched source or missing record] shows [verification issue]. I will [specific correction], then confirm [citation-reference match and claim support] before marking it resolved.

1.name: Clarify what this field is asking
1.body: The final methodological and writing changes needed before submission.
1.prompt: Which precise unresolved scholarly or writing problems remain, and how will each correction be checked?

2.name: Explain how to approach it
2.body: Record actionable corrections tied to a page, section, table or sentence, and identify the evidence or rereading needed to verify each change. Mark unresolved items accurately.
questions: What still prevents the paper from being auditable?

3.name: Compare examples and choices
3.strong_example: Action E01: reconcile the analysed n across Results and Table 1 using the log. Action E02: revise the observational conclusion's causal wording. After both changes, verify the underlying records, cross-section consistency and paragraph cohesion.
3.avoid: Avoid writing only 'proofread.'

4.name: Walk through a parallel example

walkthrough.situation: A final draft contains a Results sample count that disagrees with the analysis log, plus a conclusion that uses causal wording for an observational design.
thinking: First reconcile the sample count against the actual analysed records and every table referring to it.
Replace causal language with an inference justified by the study's observed exposure and design.
Read the revised Results and Discussion together for logical flow, then verify the corrected citations and document what remains unresolved.
walkthrough.draft: Action E01: reconcile the analysed n across Results and Table 1 using the log. Action E02: revise the observational conclusion's causal wording. After both changes, verify the underlying records, cross-section consistency and paragraph cohesion.

4.boundary: This example uses a different or generic context. Follow the reasoning sequence, not the example's answer.

5.name: Help me build my own answer
5.frame: Before submission I will correct [specific evidence or method problem] at [location] and verify it using [record]. I will revise [specific prose or citation problem] at [location], reread [surrounding context], and retain [unresolved item] for follow-up.

search.title: Search log · Record the search performed
search.body: Record a search only after you have run it. Keep its date, database, exact submitted query, search fields, filters and reported results. Proposed strings belong in the plan, and a quick unsuccessful search cannot establish that no relevant research exists.

walkthrough.situation: A student has proposed a retrieval-practice search in ERIC but has not yet submitted it.
thinking: The concept terms and Boolean string can be prepared before using the database.
Without a completed search I cannot supply a date or result count.
After execution I will copy the exact submitted string, platform settings and actual result count into the log.
walkthrough.draft: Proposed only: ("retrieval practice" OR "practice testing") AND (biology OR "science education"). Search date, filters and retrieved count remain pending until this exact query is run.

search.next_prompt: Which search will you actually run next, in which database, and what exact settings will you record? Separate planned syntax from an executed search.
search.compare_prompt: Compare a broad and a focused search route by asking which concepts they combine, what each might miss and how you would document the actual queries.

sources.title: Source record · What each paper contributes
sources.body: Record what each source actually contributes. Keep its identifier, question, design, population, measures, results and limits. Verify the paper itself before citing a statement; peer review alone does not establish relevance or measurement validity.

walkthrough.situation: A student reads an observational survey paper about study habits and memory scores.
thinking: First record the source and its actual measures without reinterpreting the result.
The design may support a reported association but cannot by itself isolate a causal effect.
Note the sample and measurement limits next to the findings so later synthesis stays faithful.
walkthrough.draft: Source record template: [verified citation and ID]; [design and sampling]; [exact measured variables]; [reported finding and page/table]; [limits on interpretation]. No findings are entered without checking the paper.

sources.next_prompt: For the source you have open, which verified design, measure and result belong in its record, and where in the paper can each be checked?
sources.compare_prompt: Compare two source types by checking what data each reports, which methods were used and what claims the source can support.

screen.title: Screening · Apply rules consistently
screen.body: Apply inclusion and exclusion criteria consistently, regardless of whether a study supports your expectation. Record a distinct decision and reason for each report, and separate uncertain abstracts from full-text decisions.

walkthrough.situation: A hypothetical screening protocol requires empirical research with a delayed learning outcome. A commentary argues that retrieval practice works.
thinking: A commentary can be relevant background but does not meet the defined empirical-evidence criterion.
The reason for exclusion is source type, not agreement or disagreement with the argument.
Record the report ID and screening stage; if eligibility is unclear, obtain further information rather than guessing.
walkthrough.draft: Hypothetical screening decision: exclude report S-02 at the appropriate screening stage because it has no original empirical data under the predefined criteria. Record its exact source ID and reason; do not count it as an included empirical study.

screen.next_prompt: Which eligibility rule determines this source's include, exclude or uncertain status, and what evidence from the record supports the decision?
screen.compare_prompt: Compare include, exclude and pending decisions against the actual eligibility criteria. A result supporting your expectation does not change those rules.

study.title: Study matrix · Compare like with like
study.body: Use the study matrix to compare the same research dimensions across sources. Record actual participant or system contexts, designs, operational measures and results before deciding whether apparent disagreements are substantively comparable.

walkthrough.situation: Two fictional studies both discuss 'retention', but one uses immediate recognition and the other delayed free recall.
thinking: The shared word 'retention' can hide different outcome definitions.
Record the assessment interval and scoring method for each study in separate matrix columns.
A direct comparison of effect size may be inappropriate until the differences are examined.
walkthrough.draft: Fictional matrix comparison: study A measures next-day recognition; study B measures free recall after a week. The matrix records distinct outcome definitions, so their estimates cannot simply be compared as interchangeable retention measures.

study.next_prompt: Which two sources or study records should be compared next, and which common matrix dimensions will show whether their outcomes are genuinely comparable?
study.compare_prompt: Compare sources using the same columns for population, design, measures and findings. Identify differences that would make direct comparison misleading.

synth.title: Synthesis · Build claims across studies
synth.body: Synthesize findings across actual sources by identifying the question they address, what the evidence supports and where it varies. Link every theme to its study records, including credible contrary or inconclusive findings.

walkthrough.situation: A fictional evidence table contains two studies using delayed recall and another using immediate recognition.
thinking: Compare studies that ask sufficiently similar questions and use relevant measures.
The different testing interval may limit whether the findings can be described as one pattern.
An evidence-based synthesis should name sources and describe the variation without inventing a field-wide consensus.
walkthrough.draft: Fictional synthesis plan: group studies A and B under delayed-recall outcomes, then discuss study C's immediate-recognition measure separately. Replace each ID with checked evidence before asserting convergence.

synth.next_prompt: Which verified sources support your emerging synthesis claim, which source complicates it, and how will you express the boundary between their methods?
synth.compare_prompt: Compare the evidence supporting a theme with studies that complicate it. Which patterns remain defensible across the relevant methods and contexts?

gap.title: Study rationale · Make the smallest defensible claim
gap.body: A study may make a useful local extension, replication or method comparison even when related research exists. Base the justification on a documented search and the evidence reviewed; never infer that a whole field lacks research from a few searches.

walkthrough.situation: A student reads university-based retrieval-practice studies and wants to investigate a similar question in one secondary classroom.
thinking: Existing research establishes that the broader question has already been examined.
The selected sources alone cannot demonstrate that all secondary-school research is absent.
A local extension is defensible if the project clearly describes its new context and evidence.
walkthrough.draft: Proposed rationale for this fictional case: examine a previously studied retrieval-practice question in one local secondary science setting, while recording the limited scope of the literature search. No global research gap is claimed.

gap.next_prompt: Which supported rationale best describes your project now, and what exact reviewed evidence justifies an extension, replication, inconsistency or local question?
gap.compare_prompt: Compare replication, extension, local inquiry and a documented literature gap. Choose the smallest rationale supported by the searches and papers actually reviewed.

claims.title: Claim audit · Match statements to evidence
claims.body: Check each literature claim against the underlying sources and its actual scope. Match in-text citations to verified references, and distinguish what a source measured from how its authors interpreted the evidence.

walkthrough.situation: A draft says that study strategies always improve grades and cites one observational survey.
thinking: The word 'always' implies broader and stronger evidence than one survey can provide.
Read the original source to identify which variables it measured and which association it reported.
Revise or remove the claim until its scope matches the verified evidence and citation.
walkthrough.draft: Unresolved claim C01: 'Study strategies always improve grades.' Verify the cited survey's measures and conclusions before replacing this with a bounded, accurate statement; do not retain an unsupported universal claim.

claims.next_prompt: Which exact sentence needs verification, which source and result will you check, and how will you document a correction or an unresolved citation?
claims.compare_prompt: Compare a precise source-supported sentence with a broader assertion that the same source does not warrant. Specify what must be checked or qualified.

outline.title: Paragraph planning · Develop coherent ideas
outline.body: Plan paragraphs around connected ideas and comparisons across sources. Give each paragraph a focused question or interpretive task, decide which verified evidence belongs there and show how it leads naturally into the next point.

walkthrough.situation: A student's literature review has three consecutive paragraphs, each giving a separate article summary.
thinking: The first two sources both address when learning was assessed, so they can be compared together.
The third differs in scoring method and may clarify why the findings are difficult to compare.
Develop the paragraph around measurement decisions and their consequences, with citations checked before drafting.
walkthrough.draft: Paragraph plan: introduce variation in assessment timing; compare verified sources using matched time intervals; qualify the comparison using differing test formats; move to the next paragraph on how outcome definitions affect interpretation.

outline.next_prompt: What is the next paragraph's intellectual task, which checked sources will develop it, and how does its reasoning connect to the preceding paragraph?
outline.compare_prompt: Compare a series of one-paper summaries with an idea-led sequence. Which paragraph structure makes relationships and transitions between sources clearer?

design.title: Study design · match claims to evidence
design.body: Identify whether a researcher assigns a condition or observes an existing difference. Specify the unit, timing, possible confounders, and the conclusions the design can reasonably support.

walkthrough.situation: A student wants to know whether sleeping longer improves quiz scores. They can record volunteered sleep logs and quiz results but cannot assign sleep duration.
thinking: Sleep duration is observed, and students may differ in preparation, health or other factors that affect quiz scores.
Repeated logs from the same student are linked observations, not independent students.
The plan can examine an association in this group; neither correlation nor repeated measurements alone establishes a sleep effect.
walkthrough.draft: Design: observational study of volunteered sleep logs and quiz scores. Unit: student, with repeated days linked by student ID. Claim: describe an association within the participating group, accounting for repeated observations and plausible confounders.

design.next_prompt: State whether your main factor is assigned or observed, identify the unit and timing, and write one conclusion your design could support without overclaiming.
design.compare_prompt: Compare an assigned-condition experiment with an observational comparison. What changes in the possible causal interpretation, and what remains dependent on the design?

vars.title: Variables and constructs · specify observable records
vars.body: Translate the research question into constructs and recorded variables. Name the predictor, exposure or assigned factor as appropriate; define each measure, its scale, timing and unit.

walkthrough.situation: A student plans to compare 'stress' with 'performance' using a voluntary survey and a defined quiz.
thinking: Stress and performance are constructs until the measures and timing are specified.
A reported stress score is an observed predictor, not an assigned experimental treatment.
The questionnaire and quiz can capture only the aspects of these constructs that their items actually measure.
walkthrough.draft: Observed predictor: score on a named stress questionnaire completed before the quiz. Outcome: correct answers out of 20 on the specified quiz. Unit: consenting participant; record collection date and a coded participant ID.

vars.next_prompt: For each main construct, name the exact record, instrument or rule, scale, timing and unit; identify whether the factor is assigned or observed.
vars.compare_prompt: Compare a broad construct with an operationally defined record. Which version could another researcher collect consistently, and what meaning might the measure leave out?

rep.title: Units and replication · distinguish repeated readings
rep.body: Identify the unit independently assigned to a treatment, if applicable, and the unit observed. Separate independently replicated units from subsamples, technical repeats and repeated measurements; preserve their identifiers.

walkthrough.situation: A student places 20 seeds in each of two dishes, assigning one dish to water and the other to salt solution.
thinking: Treatment is assigned to a whole dish; individual seeds share that dish's conditions.
The 20 seeds provide subsample measurements within each dish, not 20 independent treatment assignments.
With only one dish per condition, any apparent treatment difference is confounded with dish-level differences; additional independently assigned dishes would be needed for treatment replication.
walkthrough.draft: Experimental unit: dish. Observation: seed germination within dish. Record dish_id and seed_id; increase the number of independently assigned dishes per condition before estimating a treatment effect.

rep.next_prompt: Identify the treatment-assignment unit and observation unit, then explain which records are independent replicates and which are repeated or nested observations.
rep.compare_prompt: Compare 20 seeds in one treated dish with seeds distributed among several independently treated dishes. Which count supports treatment replication, and why?

sample.title: Sampling · specify who or what is represented
sample.body: State the target population, actual sampling frame, inclusion rules and recruitment process. Separate random sampling for representativeness from random assignment for comparisons, and limit generalization accordingly.

walkthrough.situation: A student invites volunteers from one biology class and hopes to describe study habits across all teenagers.
thinking: One accessible class is not a random selection of teenagers.
Volunteers may differ from classmates who do not participate.
Findings can describe participating students; extension to other schools or age groups would require further evidence.
walkthrough.draft: Sampling frame: students in one accessible class. Recruitment: voluntary convenience sample under school procedures. Report the number invited and participating; avoid claims of national representativeness.

sample.next_prompt: Write your target population, actual sampling frame, inclusion criteria and recruitment approach, then set a defensible boundary for generalization.
sample.compare_prompt: Compare a convenience sample from one class with a randomly selected sample from a defined school roster. What population could each plausibly represent?

measure.title: Measurement · define how evidence is recorded
measure.body: For every outcome or predictor, specify the instrument or procedure, scoring rule, unit or category, time point, and quality checks. Consider measurement validity, consistency and relevant calibration without assuming they are established.

walkthrough.situation: A student wants to measure plant growth and proposes writing 'grew well' after each observation.
thinking: 'Grew well' has no reproducible scoring rule and may mix height, leaf condition and colour.
Plant height in centimetres can be recorded from a stated reference point at consistent times, though height alone is not all of growth.
A repeat-measurement check and a consistent ruler procedure may reveal recording variation; neither guarantees that height captures every aspect of plant development.
walkthrough.draft: Measure stem height (cm) from soil surface to the highest stem point with a ruler at the same scheduled time each week. Record plant_id, date, height_cm and any measurement difficulty; document the ruler and procedure.

measure.next_prompt: Choose one key variable and specify the instrument, precise scoring or measurement rule, units, timing and one way to evaluate the quality of the record.
measure.compare_prompt: Compare a loosely rated 'healthy plant' score with a defined leaf-count procedure. What is gained in consistency and what information about plant health may be lost?

ethics.title: Ethics and safety · establish permission before collection
ethics.body: Identify who may be affected, what information or intervention is involved, foreseeable risks, privacy protections, voluntary participation and required school or institutional approvals. Teacher access is not itself research permission.

walkthrough.situation: A student wants to obtain classmates' quiz scores and interview them about study habits for a public project.
thinking: Routine access to grades does not authorize their reuse for research, and students could feel pressured to participate.
The student must consult the teacher and applicable school procedures before approaching participants, especially if minors are involved.
A non-identifiable, approved aggregate approach may reduce privacy risks, but it does not automatically remove all approval or consent obligations.
walkthrough.draft: Before collection, consult the responsible teacher and school policy about required review, permission and student/guardian consent or assent. Do not access individual grades or conduct interviews until authorization is documented; plan data minimization, secure storage and withdrawal procedures.

ethics.next_prompt: Identify whose data or participation you need, relevant risks, approvals and consent procedures, and one safer alternative if permission is unavailable.
ethics.compare_prompt: Compare a class assignment using anonymous aggregate counts with a project collecting identifiable student responses. What additional permissions, protections or alternatives may be needed?

procedure.title: Procedure · make each step reproducible
procedure.body: Describe preparation, assignment or selection, measurements, timing, recording and deviations in order. Specify decisions another researcher would otherwise need to guess, while keeping safety and approval requirements explicit.

walkthrough.situation: A student writes, 'Put seedlings in light, water them and measure them for two weeks.'
thinking: The plan omits initial selection, light placement, water amounts and when the measurements occur.
The same measuring point and a schedule help make successive records comparable.
Missed watering or a moved pot should be recorded as a deviation rather than silently corrected in the final report.
walkthrough.draft: Label each plant and record its starting height. Specify light conditions and watering amount and schedule. Measure height in centimetres from the stated reference point on days 0, 7 and 14; log any missed step or change in conditions.

procedure.next_prompt: Write the ordered steps someone else could follow, including timing, materials, recording rules and how deviations will be documented.
procedure.compare_prompt: Compare 'water plants regularly and measure growth' with a procedure specifying amounts, intervals, measurement rules and deviation logs. Which decisions affect replication?

data.title: Data table · define rows, identifiers and codes
data.body: Define the meaning of one row before creating columns. Include identifiers that preserve grouping and time, specify units and allowed categories, and distinguish missing observations from measured zeroes.

walkthrough.situation: A student measures seeds nested within dishes over three dates and plans a spreadsheet headed only 'height.'
thinking: A height value without an identifier cannot be linked reliably to its seed, dish or date.
Repeated records from one seed and seeds from one dish are linked rather than independent.
An empty cell needs a documented meaning; zero growth and a missing measurement must remain distinguishable.
walkthrough.draft: One row = one seed on one observation date. Columns: dish_id, seed_id, date, treatment, height_cm and observation_status. Record a missing measurement with a documented status, not 0 cm.

data.next_prompt: Define exactly what one row represents and draft the essential column names, identifiers, units, category codes and missing-data rule.
data.compare_prompt: Compare a table with only seed height values with one containing dish_id, seed_id, day, height_cm and a missing-value code. Which supports valid grouping and checks?

audit.title: Plan audit · check decisions before data collection
audit.body: Review the question-to-evidence chain for contradictions among design, sampling, units, measures, procedures, analysis and permissions. Preserve a dated plan version before examining final outcomes, and document later changes transparently.

walkthrough.situation: A student completes a plan for comparing plant treatments, then notices that it lists 20 seeds per dish as 20 independent treatment replicates.
thinking: The plan's unit count contradicts its actual dish-level treatment assignment.
The analysis and sample-size statement must be corrected before data collection, not concealed after results appear.
The student should also check that the revised replication plan, data structure, safety arrangements and analysis all agree, then save a dated version.
walkthrough.draft: Pre-collection audit: treatment unit = dish; seeds are nested observations. Revise replication and analysis accordingly, confirm required approvals, and save dated protocol v2 with a brief change record before collecting data.

audit.next_prompt: Identify the weakest link between your question, design, units, measurements, analysis and permissions; document the correction and version of the plan.
audit.compare_prompt: Compare a dated, approved study plan with one rewritten after reviewing outcomes. How does the version history affect interpretation of the analysis?

import.title: Import · preserve and trace the raw records
import.body: Preserve an unchanged source file before making corrections. Record where the file came from, when it was exported, what one row represents, and how identifiers preserve repeated, paired or nested observations. Keep access to identifiable records restricted.

walkthrough.situation: A student imports weekly plant measurements from a file in which plant IDs such as 007 may be converted to 7.
thinking: The source records should remain unchanged so that accidental conversions can be investigated.
I need to preserve plant IDs as identifiers, retain their links to observation dates, and confirm that each imported row still matches its source.
I will make corrections in a separate analysis copy, documenting what changed and why; identifiable information, if present, needs appropriate storage controls.
walkthrough.draft: Import log: save an unmodified source export with its date and location. Create a working copy, treat plant_id as text, check row counts and plant-date matches, and record any corrected import formats.

import.next_prompt: Identify your raw source, the meaning of each row and its identifiers, then state how you will preserve the original and document changes.
import.compare_prompt: Compare editing the original spreadsheet with making a dated working copy and recording each transformation. Which process allows someone to trace a later discrepancy?

quality.title: Data quality · investigate anomalies before changing records
quality.body: Check missing observations, duplicates, coding conflicts, impossible values and extreme measurements against the source and data dictionary. Distinguish confirmed mistakes from plausible observations; document every correction or exclusion.

walkthrough.situation: In a plant-height file, one value is 91 cm while neighbouring measurements are near 9 cm.
thinking: The difference makes the value worth checking, but magnitude alone cannot establish an error.
I will compare the entry with the original record, units and field notes. If the original shows 9.1 cm, I can correct the transcription and keep an audit trail.
If the source truly records 91 cm, I should preserve it, investigate the measurement context and explain any sensitivity analysis rather than deleting it for a preferred result.
walkthrough.draft: Quality log: flag plant_id and date; verify against the source. Record either a source-supported correction with old and new values, or a retained extreme value with the reason for keeping it.

quality.next_prompt: Select one missing, duplicate, inconsistent or unusual record. State how you will check its source and document the decision before making changes.
quality.compare_prompt: Compare a documented transcription error with an extreme measurement confirmed by the source. What action would be justified for each, and what evidence would you retain?

explore.title: Explore · examine distributions and linked observations
explore.body: Choose summaries and displays suited to the outcome and unit structure. Inspect numerical distributions and relationships, categorical counts with denominators, and paired or repeated trajectories without treating linked observations as independent.

walkthrough.situation: The same students complete a short quiz before and after a workshop, and their average score rises.
thinking: A higher average does not show whether nearly all students improved or a few large changes drove the mean.
I will link each student's two scores and inspect a paired-point or connected-line plot; I will also count missing pre- or post-scores.
The display describes observed score changes and does not, by itself, show that the workshop caused them.
walkthrough.draft: Exploration plan: one paired record per student with before_score and after_score. Plot connected student scores and the distribution of within-student changes; report complete pairs and missing measurements.

explore.next_prompt: Name the variable type and observation structure, then choose one display and one summary that reveal features a single overall average might miss.
explore.compare_prompt: Compare a single mean change with a plot showing each student's paired scores. What individual patterns would the mean conceal?

setup.title: Analysis setup · define the target and evidence structure
setup.body: For quantitative work, specify the quantity of interest, outcome type, independent or paired units, and any clustering before selecting a method. For qualitative work, specify the phenomenon and interpretive question rather than imposing a numerical estimand.

walkthrough.situation: The same students answer a correct/incorrect question before and after a teaching activity.
thinking: Correct/incorrect is a binary outcome, and the two records from each student form a pair.
The quantitative target might be the difference between the before and after proportions correct. The paired transition counts explain that difference.

A McNemar-type test evaluates whether the two discordant transition directions differ, under its assumptions. Neither the paired comparison nor its p-value alone establishes that the activity caused a change.
walkthrough.draft: Outcome: correct/incorrect for each student at two time points. Structure: paired binary. Target: within-sample difference in proportions correct; tabulate incorrect-to-correct and correct-to-incorrect transitions, then consider a suitable paired method.

setup.next_prompt: Write the outcome type, the observation unit and any repeated or nested structure. State your quantitative target or qualitative interpretive question before choosing an analysis.

run.title: Run analysis · match columns to independent units
run.body: Confirm that selected variables, grouping codes, exclusions and analysis units match the design. Check the method's assumptions and warnings before interpreting the output; a calculation cannot repair incorrectly counted independent units.

walkthrough.situation: A student independently assigns four trays to each of three fertiliser conditions, with five seedlings measured within every tray.
thinking: Each tray receives one fertiliser condition. The five seedlings measured within a tray share that treatment assignment.
Treating all seedling heights as independent treatment replicates would overstate replication. Tray-level summaries or a model accounting for trays may be appropriate for the planned question.
Before any mean comparison, I need to map treatment codes and outcome units correctly, inspect the distribution and variability, and choose a method whose assumptions fit the actual data.
walkthrough.draft: Analysis mapping: treatment = assigned fertiliser; primary replication unit = tray, four trays per condition. Retain tray_id and seedling_id; assess a tray-level comparison or a clustered model, checking assumptions and reporting uncertainty.

run.next_prompt: State the exact outcome and grouping columns, the independent or clustered unit count, the method chosen and which diagnostic or warning must be checked.

history.title: Analysis record · keep every consequential choice traceable
history.body: Save primary and exploratory analysis versions with dataset identifiers, selected columns, exclusions, method settings, diagnostics and outputs. Report estimates and uncertainty when appropriate, and explain changes instead of selecting the smallest p-value.

walkthrough.situation: A student reruns a correlation after excluding two unusual observations and gets a different p-value.
thinking: I need to establish whether the exclusions were specified in advance or followed inspection of the result.
Both analyses should remain in the history with their datasets, sample sizes, reasons for exclusions and relevant diagnostics.
The primary and sensitivity results can be compared transparently; I should not relabel whichever produces the smallest p-value as the original analysis.
walkthrough.draft: Analysis history: run A uses all source-verified eligible observations; run B excludes two observations only under a documented rule. Retain both outputs, variable mappings, diagnostics, sample sizes and the reason for comparing them.

history.next_prompt: Identify your primary saved analysis, its data version and settings, then document any alternative run and why it was performed.
history.compare_prompt: Compare keeping only the most favourable result with recording the primary analysis and later justified sensitivity checks. What can a reader evaluate in each record?

audit.title: Results audit · reconnect findings to the original question
audit.body: Check that the reported participants or units, analysis sample, target quantity, result and uncertainty agree with the study plan. Identify unsupported generalizations, unreported exclusions and causal language that exceeds the design.

walkthrough.situation: A student surveys 18 volunteers on two dates. Their report calls the 36 survey rows '36 independent students' and claims the course caused an attitude shift.
thinking: There are 36 responses from 18 people, so the analysis and reported sample must preserve paired student IDs.
The survey can document patterns or changes within these volunteers, subject to missingness and measurement limitations.
Without a design that supports causal attribution, the result cannot establish that the course produced the reported shift; the wording and analysis must be corrected.
walkthrough.draft: Audit note: 18 volunteers contributed up to two responses each. Recheck completeness and use a paired or repeated analysis if appropriate. Report the observed attitude pattern without attributing it causally to the course.

audit.next_prompt: Compare your reported sample, units, estimate and claim with your design and analysis record; identify and correct one mismatch before finalizing Results.
audit.compare_prompt: Compare a report of 36 independent students with records from 18 students measured twice. How would correcting the unit count change the result description and its uncertainty?

intro.title: Introduction · lead the reader to a defensible question
intro.body: Introduce the phenomenon and the specific question through relevant context and checked research. Explain how the evidence supports the rationale, then state the study's purpose without claiming that a gap or novelty has already been established.

walkthrough.situation: A student proposes observing pollinators around a school garden and begins, 'No one has studied pollinators in schools.' They have read only two papers.
thinking: Two papers cannot establish that no previous research exists.
I need to identify the phenomenon, the particular school setting and what the reviewed sources actually examined.
The introduction can explain the local purpose and relevant prior evidence while leaving any broader claim of novelty unresolved.
walkthrough.draft: Proposed study purpose: document pollinator visits in the school garden during defined observation periods. Describe the local setting and relevant checked studies, then state the research question without asserting an unverified literature gap.

intro.next_prompt: Draft the specific phenomenon, source-supported context and purpose that lead to your question. Mark any proposed gap that still requires verification.
intro.compare_prompt: Compare 'No one has studied this topic' with a rationale based on a documented difference between the student's context and the settings in the sources reviewed. Which claim can the evidence actually support?

lit.title: Literature review · connect claims across verified sources
lit.body: Organise paragraphs around substantive relationships among studies, such as differences in participants, measures, settings or interpretations. Support each comparison with the actual sources, and distinguish what they report from your synthesis.

walkthrough.situation: Two hypothetical papers both use the word 'engagement'. One measures self-reported interest and the other counts contributions during lessons.
thinking: The common label does not mean that the two studies measured the same outcome.
I should first verify how each author defined and recorded engagement, including the setting and participants.
A useful synthesis explains why the measures capture different aspects of participation and does not invent agreement or a shared effect.
walkthrough.draft: Comparative note for source verification: one study operationalises engagement through self-reported interest, while the other counts classroom contributions. Compare their definitions and settings before drawing any conclusion across the two sources.

lit.next_prompt: Select two verified sources, identify a meaningful connection or difference between them, and write a comparison that respects what each actually measured or described.
lit.compare_prompt: Compare separate summaries of two studies with a paragraph that explains how their definitions and methods permit or restrict comparison. What should the reader learn from the relationship?

method.title: Method · report the work with procedural fidelity
method.body: For completed research, describe the setting, participants or materials, sampling, instruments, procedures and analysis as actually undertaken. Disclose departures from the plan. For a proposal, use prospective language and keep permissions and uncompleted actions clearly identified.

walkthrough.situation: A student's approved classroom observation plan specified ten observation days, but the project logs document only seven because the room was unavailable for three.
thinking: Reporting ten completed sessions would misrepresent what happened.
I need to check the approved plan against dated observation logs and report the seven sessions actually conducted.
If the change affects coverage or interpretation, the Method and limitations should explain its consequences.
walkthrough.draft: The plan specified ten observation days. Seven observation sessions were completed; three planned sessions could not take place because the room was unavailable. The analysis drew on the seven recorded sessions.

method.next_prompt: Identify a procedure, sample or analysis step that readers need to reproduce or evaluate. Confirm whether it was planned, completed or changed, and draft wording consistent with the records.
method.compare_prompt: Compare a Methods section that silently repeats the original plan with one that records the procedure actually used and explains deviations. Which allows another reader to evaluate the evidence?

results.title: Results · present traceable observations and patterns
results.body: Report the analysed sample or corpus, descriptive observations, central results and relevant uncertainty using the appropriate evidence records. When Results and Discussion are separate, reserve broader explanations for Discussion, while allowing grounded interpretation within qualitative Findings.

walkthrough.situation: In a hypothetical dataset of 20 students with complete before-and-after scores, 12 scores increased, five stayed the same, and three decreased.
thinking: All 20 paired observations belong in the result, including unchanged and lower scores.
I should report counts with the denominator and connect the statement to the recorded paired differences.
These descriptive results alone do not show that the teaching activity caused the observed changes.
walkthrough.draft: Among 20 students with paired scores, 12 scored higher at the second measurement, five had unchanged scores, and three scored lower. Report the score-change distribution alongside the corresponding table or plot.

results.next_prompt: Choose a primary finding and trace every count, estimate or theme to its source. Write a Results passage that includes the appropriate denominator and uncertainty or evidence excerpt.
results.compare_prompt: Compare a result that states only 'scores improved' with one that reports the paired counts, denominator and where the data appear. Which wording permits a reader to assess the pattern?

discussion.title: Discussion · interpret findings within their limits
discussion.body: Begin with an answer to the research question supported by the findings. Develop plausible interpretations and alternatives, relate them to checked research, and explain how limitations restrict the resulting claims rather than listing weaknesses without consequences.

walkthrough.situation: A schoolyard survey records more bee visits in sunnier plots, but sunnier plots were also observed at a different time of day.
thinking: The observations support a pattern linking recorded visits with plot conditions in the sampled periods.
Time of day may affect bee activity and is entangled with the plot comparison, so sunlight cannot be isolated as the cause.
The discussion should identify this alternative explanation and limit any recommendation or future study proposal accordingly.
walkthrough.draft: Bee visits were more frequent in the sunnier plots during the observations. Because plot conditions and observation times varied together, these records do not establish that sunlight alone produced the difference.

discussion.next_prompt: Write your strongest supported answer to the question, then explain one alternative interpretation and one limitation that materially changes the conclusion.
discussion.compare_prompt: Compare a Discussion that calls an observational pattern an effect with one that considers observation timing and environmental differences. How does each treatment of alternatives change the claim?

closing.title: Conclusion and abstract · reflect completed or proposed work
closing.body: Return to the research question with a conclusion bounded by the available evidence. An abstract for completed work summarises its purpose, approach, principal findings and conclusion; a proposal describes the intended inquiry without reporting imagined results.

walkthrough.situation: A student has proposed a three-week comparison of seedling heights under two light settings, but the draft abstract says the study demonstrated faster growth.
thinking: The proposed measurements have not been collected, so no comparative result is available.
The abstract can specify the planned system, duration, measures and question using future-facing language.
The conclusion of a proposal should describe its intended contribution or scope, not an outcome presented as established.
walkthrough.draft: This proposed study will compare seedling stem-height records collected over three weeks under two documented light settings. Data collection and results remain pending.

closing.next_prompt: State whether the work is proposed or completed. Draft a bounded concluding answer and an abstract sentence that accurately reflects which findings, if any, are available.
closing.compare_prompt: Compare an abstract that says a proposed study 'demonstrated' an effect with one that reports the planned observations and clearly states that results are unavailable. Which accurately reflects the project's status?

citations.title: Citation audit · check every source-to-claim link
citations.body: Confirm that each citation identifies a real, accessible source and that the cited passage supports the exact claim, population and strength of language used. Check quotation fidelity, bibliographic details and references that appear without corresponding text citations.

walkthrough.situation: A paper states that 'all teachers prefer group work' and cites a study reporting interviews with six teachers at one school.
thinking: Six interviews at one school cannot establish a preference shared by all teachers.
I must inspect the original study and determine what each interview actually reported before deciding whether any collective statement is warranted.
The revised claim needs a precise scope and a complete, verified reference; an unsupported universal statement should be removed.
walkthrough.draft: Citation check C01: verify the six interview accounts and their context. Replace 'all teachers' only with a description the source actually supports, or remove the claim. Confirm the citation and reference match.

citations.next_prompt: Choose one substantive claim and its citation. Verify the original passage, scope and reference details, then record whether you kept, qualified, replaced or removed the claim.
citations.compare_prompt: Compare a population-wide claim cited to interviews from one school with a source-bound statement of what those interviews actually documented. What wording can the checked source support?

audit.title: Whole-paper audit · trace every claim to its evidence
audit.body: Compare the question, literature, design, collected evidence, analysis, findings and final claims as one continuous argument. Detect mismatched units, unsupported inference, inconsistent statuses, missing records and revisions that create contradictions elsewhere in the paper.

walkthrough.situation: A research question asks how students negotiate scientific explanations in group talk, but the completed study collected only individual written responses.
thinking: Written responses can show what individual students represented on the page; they do not document the interaction through which groups negotiated an explanation.
The completed Method and Results must not imply that conversations were recorded or analysed.
I should narrow the research question to the available written evidence, or identify group interaction as a separate question requiring a new authorised study.
walkthrough.draft: Evidence-chain correction: revise the question to examine scientific explanations in the collected individual written responses. Do not claim to analyse group negotiation without interactional records.

audit.next_prompt: Trace one major conclusion back through Results, analysis, evidence, Method and question. Identify where the chain breaks and draft a correction that can be applied consistently.
audit.compare_prompt: Compare a question about group negotiation with a method that records only private written answers. What can those records answer, and what evidence is missing for the original question?
